props.title: Volcano

sections.content: Volcano erupted during the peak of 90s disaster films, following the massive success of Twister (1996) and competing directly with Dante's Peak (1997). Tommy Lee Jones leads as the LA emergency chief battling an unprecedented crisis when a volcanic vent opens under Los Angeles. While scientifically dubious, the film delivers intense urban destruction sequences that hold up surprisingly well, mixing practical effects with then-cutting-edge CGI. It follows the disaster movie formula established by The Towering Inferno (1974) and perfected by Independence Day (1996): multiple storylines, a diverse cast of characters, and escalating catastrophes leading to a heroic finale.

movies.slug: Pierce Brosnan stars as a volcanologist trying to save a small town from an awakening volcano. More scientifically accurate than Volcano.

sections.content: The 1990s disaster revival marked a significant shift in how Hollywood approached catastrophe films. Deep Impact (1998) and Armageddon (1998) took the destruction global, while Volcano and Dante's Peak kept threats localized but intensely personal. These films established a template still used today in movies like Greenland (2020) and Moonfall (2022): focusing on both the spectacle of destruction and intimate family drama against impossible odds. SUBHEAD: Urban Disaster Films

Volcano sits within a rich tradition of Los Angeles-destruction films, from Earthquake (1974) to 2012 (2009). The city's unique geography, architecture, and cultural significance make it an ideal setting for disaster scenarios. The film's memorable scene of lava flowing down Wilshire Boulevard taps into primal fears about urban vulnerability, similar to how The Day After Tomorrow (2004) froze New York and Battle: Los Angeles (2011) turned LA into a war zone.
